## Design

### 2026-11-01: I decided to create a desk screen thing that showcases the current music playing and the info about the music playing. Similar to how it would show up on Apple CarPlay or Android Auto. I came up with

**3h**

I decided to create a desk screen thing that showcases the current music playing and the info about the music playing. Similar to how it would show up on Apple CarPlay or Android Auto. I came up with this idea mainly to make sure I can control my music while studying without getting distracted because I need to open up my phone to change songs or something.

I started by making the schematic. I am going to directly solder the TFT Touch Screen to the PCB, and will try to make the whole thing fit the size of the screen so when I make a case it can be as small as possible. In general, there were not many components, just the screen and a rotary encoder. However, it took me a while to figure out how to do the TFT touch screen, as I had never worked with it before. I also used some AI to understand what each of the pins does and what kind of control they need. Then I wired the rotary encoder. I chose to use the ESP32 Super Mini so it can fit my size restrictions and it has enough GPIO pins.

I started with an unpolished version: just connect the right pins to the right pins on the screen's connector, then I moved to adding the EC11 Rotary Encoder, and then I polished it up. I did use Claude to generate the schematic symbol and footprint for the ESP32 Super Mini, as I could not find that in any of the existing libraries or online.

### 2026-11-01: I started making the layout of the PCB and the routing. To do this, I first had to set the footprints of each of the components. I started off with SMD resistors like the image shows, but later switch

**4h**

I started making the layout of the PCB and the routing. To do this, I first had to set the footprints of each of the components. I started off with SMD resistors like the image shows, but later switched to THT resistors as they are easier to solder and use. I also found out that I already have some, so I figured why buy more.

![AssignedFootprints](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/c90af68b74cd55bc7895a82e4f3fbd94f2b168f708c0e84a5f51c9c58000d3f1.png)

I originally based my layout on what the size of the screen will be, a 2.8" screen, and where I want the encoder to go. I put the encoder in such a way that it wouldn't interfere with the screen. And I put the ESP32 Super Mini close to the connector holes for the screen to allow for the easiest routing. Then I spent a long time doing all of the routing, and it took longer than usual because I wanted it to look neat, so I also spent a lot of time changing which GPIO pins of the ESP32 the screen connects to for the cleanest wiring.

![OldRouting](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/5485bec3407a2e4ba10c2813e75dda595f39f9d59a25a7eafdca42b3dad8567e.png)

Then I realized that even though I put the ESP32 at the back, the pin headers that will get soldered will still stick out of the back, and I don't know how high up the screen would sit, so I assumed they would be hitting. So I moved the ESP32 below the screen, but this meant rerouting the entire board and again changing which GPIO pin each screen pin connects to. And the rotary encoder pins. This took a really long time as well.
Here is the finished routing and the 3D views of the PCB:

![NewRouting](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Gh41LCklf8pAFUOLAd0zqSVIN2Jmcw6K/2456c436450dd0e1c2f8c963dcba3555fc7f540472c98fa94a3e62673e1e3440.png)

### 2026-11-01: I worked on making my BOM. I selected the ESP32 Super Mini, the TFT touchscreen, the rotary encoder, and the PCB. The TFT took the longest time because I had to find one with a touchscreen that was th

**0.5h**

I worked on making my BOM. I selected the ESP32 Super Mini, the TFT touchscreen, the rotary encoder, and the PCB. The TFT took the longest time because I had to find one with a touchscreen that was the appropriate size, and was not insanely expensive. I then worked to find the ESP32, which didn't take as long. For the rotary encoder, I picked the same one I did for previous projects. And then the PCB was just using the fabrication tool in KiCad to get all the right files and then placing the JLCPCB order.
